title: Belgrade Breaks with Pale: Milosevic Cuts the Lifeline
content:
Throughout the first two years of the Bosnian War, the relationship between Belgrade and Pale had been the essential axis of the Bosnian Serb war effort. Serbia under Slobodan Milosevic provided the Republika Srpska with military supplies, fuel, financial support, and the political backing of a recognized state. Officers from the Yugoslav Army served in VRS formations. Ammunition flowed across the Drina. Without this lifeline, the Bosnian Serb entity — landlocked, internationally unrecognized, and under comprehensive UN sanctions — could not have sustained a war on multiple fronts. In August 1994, Milosevic moved to sever that connection, or at least to appear to do so.

The proximate cause was the Contact Group peace plan. Presented in July 1994 by the United States, Russia, Britain, France, and Germany, the plan proposed a territorial division giving the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina fifty-one percent of the country and Republika Srpska forty-nine percent. The Bosnian government and the Bosnian Croats accepted under intense pressure. The Bosnian Serb leadership, which controlled approximately seventy percent of Bosnian territory at the time, rejected the plan. Radovan Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb assembly calculated that the military situation favoured continued resistance over a settlement that would require surrendering roughly a third of their holdings.

Milosevic saw the matter differently. Serbia was suffering under international sanctions imposed in 1992. The Serbian economy had experienced hyperinflation of catastrophic proportions. Milosevic's priority was sanctions relief, and the Contact Group plan offered a path toward it — but only if the Bosnian Serbs cooperated. When Pale refused, Milosevic announced the closure of the border between Serbia and Republika Srpska to all goods except food, clothing, and medicine. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 942 in September 1994, tightening sanctions specifically on the Bosnian Serb entity.

The reality of the embargo was more ambiguous than the announcement suggested. International monitors deployed to the border reported that while the flow of military supplies was reduced, it was not eliminated. Smuggling continued through various channels. The VRS had stockpiled significant quantities of ammunition and equipment during the preceding years, and its immediate operational capacity was not crippled. Nevertheless, the embargo had real consequences. Fuel shortages affected VRS logistics and mobility. Spare parts for heavy equipment became scarce. The longer-term trajectory of supply was clearly downward.

The political impact cut deeper than the material one. The Bosnian Serb leadership found itself isolated not only from the international community but from its own patron state. The rupture between Belgrade and Pale exposed a fault line that had existed since the war's outset: Milosevic's war aims were not identical to those of Karadzic and Mladic. Milosevic sought a settlement that would preserve Serbian influence and lift sanctions; the Bosnian Serb leadership pursued maximalist territorial goals regardless of the diplomatic cost. The ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment examined this relationship extensively, documenting how the divergence between Belgrade and Pale evolved from policy disagreement into open confrontation.

For the VRS, the embargo meant that the war had to be fought increasingly from internal resources — captured equipment, local ammunition production, and whatever could be smuggled across an imperfectly sealed border. For the soldiers on the front lines, the political quarrel between their leaders and Belgrade was an abstraction; the dwindling supply of shells and fuel was not. The embargo did not end the war or force the Bosnian Serbs to the negotiating table in 1994. But it accelerated the erosion of VRS capability that would become decisive in the campaigns of 1995.
